title: RAM, ROM and Storage: What the Numbers on Your Phone and Laptop Really Mean
topic: công nghệ: RAM, ROM và bộ nhớ lưu trữ
summary: Why your phone's "ROM" isn't really ROM, what RAM actually does, how flash and SSDs fit in, and how much of each you need when you buy a phone or laptop.
body:
Open the specification sheet of almost any phone sold in Vietnam and you will see two numbers side by side: something like "8 GB RAM, 256 GB ROM." Walk into a computer shop and the salesperson will talk about "16 gigs of RAM" and "a 1 TB SSD." Read an article about embedded electronics and you will meet EEPROM, NOR flash and firmware. All of these words describe memory, but they describe very different kinds of memory doing very different jobs, and the everyday shorthand, especially the habit of calling a phone's storage "ROM", hides more than it explains.

This guide untangles it. By the end you should be able to explain to a friend what RAM actually is, what ROM originally meant and what it means now, why your phone's "ROM" is not really ROM, how storage fits in, and how to decide how much of each you need when you buy a phone or a laptop.

## The one-sentence version

If you remember only one thing, remember this:

- **RAM** is the computer's *working desk*: fast, temporary space where the programs and files you are using right now are laid out. It forgets everything when the power goes off.
- **ROM**, in the strict sense, is *permanent instructions printed into the machine*: a small amount of memory that holds the code a device needs to start up, and that is rarely or never changed.
- **Storage** (SSD, hard drive, or the flash chip in your phone) is the *filing cabinet*: slower, much larger, and it keeps your files, apps and photos when the power is off.

The confusion comes from the fact that phone makers use "ROM" to mean the third thing. We will come back to why.

## A desk, a filing cabinet and a rulebook

Imagine an accountant in a small office.

Her **filing cabinet** holds every document the business has ever produced: thousands of folders. It is big and it keeps things safely overnight, but getting a folder out of it takes time. That is storage.

Her **desk** is where she spreads out the folders she is working on today. She can glance from one paper to another instantly. The bigger the desk, the more folders she can have open at once without constantly walking back to the cabinet. At the end of the day the cleaner sweeps the desk clear; anything she did not file away is gone. That is RAM.

Taped to the wall is a laminated card with the office's opening routine: unlock the door, switch on the lights, open the cabinet, start work. Nobody edits it; it is the same every morning. That is ROM.

Now picture what happens when the desk is too small. She opens a fifth folder and there is no room, so she has to put one folder back in the cabinet, and when she needs it again she walks back to fetch it. Work slows to a crawl. This is exactly what a computer with too little RAM feels like: the machine is not "broken", it is constantly shuffling data between the fast desk and the slow cabinet.

## RAM: the fast, forgetful workspace

### What "random access" means

RAM stands for **random-access memory**. "Random access" sounds vague, but it means something specific: the computer can jump straight to any location in the memory and read it in roughly the same time, no matter where it is. Compare that with an old cassette tape, where to reach a song in the middle you had to wind through everything before it. That is *sequential* access.

Strictly speaking, most modern storage is also randomly accessible, so the name is partly historical. What really defines RAM today is that it is the memory the processor works in directly: it is fast, it is read and written constantly, and in its common forms it is **volatile**, meaning it loses its contents when power is removed.

### How DRAM stores a bit

The RAM in your laptop and phone is almost always **DRAM**, dynamic RAM. Each bit is stored in a tiny cell made of one transistor and one capacitor. Think of the capacitor as a microscopic bucket: charged means 1, empty means 0. The transistor is the tap that lets the computer fill or check the bucket.

The catch is that these buckets leak. Within a fraction of a second the charge drains away. So the memory chip must constantly **refresh** itself: read every cell and write the value back, over and over. Industry standards from JEDEC, the body that sets memory specifications, require each row of a typical DRAM chip to be refreshed within 64 milliseconds under normal temperatures (more often when the chip runs hot). This constant refreshing is why it is called *dynamic*, and why DRAM needs power all the time to keep its contents. Unplug it and within moments the data is gone.

The one-transistor DRAM cell was invented by Robert Dennard at IBM; he came up with the idea in 1966 and received a patent in 1968. Intel's 1103, released in 1970, was the first commercially successful DRAM chip; it held 1,024 bits. A single DRAM chip today holds billions of bits, and a laptop memory module packs many of those chips together.

### SRAM, the faster cousin

There is another kind, **SRAM** (static RAM), which stores each bit using a small circuit of usually six transistors that holds its state without refreshing as long as power is on. SRAM is much faster than DRAM but takes much more space per bit and costs more. So it is used in small quantities where speed matters most: the **cache** inside the processor itself. When you see a CPU advertised with "32 MB of L3 cache", that is SRAM sitting right next to the processor cores, holding the data they are most likely to need next.

So inside one computer there is already a hierarchy: a few megabytes of very fast SRAM cache, several gigabytes of DRAM main memory, and hundreds of gigabytes or terabytes of storage. Each step down is bigger, cheaper per gigabyte and slower.

### DDR, LPDDR and what the numbers mean

When you shop for a laptop you will see labels like **DDR4-3200**, **DDR5-5600** or **LPDDR5X-7500**.

- **DDR** stands for *double data rate*: the memory transfers data on both the rising and falling edge of each clock tick. The number after the dash is the rate in mega-transfers per second.
- **DDR4** became common in the mid-2010s. **DDR5**, whose specification JEDEC published in July 2020, is the current standard for desktops and many laptops. Each generation roughly increases speed and capacity per module and lowers voltage. The generations are not interchangeable: a DDR5 module physically will not fit a DDR4 slot.
- **LPDDR** (*low-power* DDR) is the variant used in phones, tablets and thin laptops. It is designed to sip power and is usually soldered directly onto the motherboard, which means it **cannot be upgraded later**. That detail matters a great deal when you buy a laptop, as we will see.

A rough sense of speed: a single 64-bit channel of DDR5-5600 can move about 45 gigabytes per second. Many computers use two channels in parallel ("dual channel"), doubling that bandwidth. This is why it is usually better to have two 8 GB modules than one 16 GB module in a desktop: you get the same capacity but twice the lanes.

### Why more RAM makes a computer feel faster (up to a point)

Every program you open, every browser tab, every photo you edit, needs space on the desk. Your operating system itself takes a chunk before you open anything. A modern web browser can use several hundred megabytes for a handful of tabs, and complex web apps more. Photo and video editors, games and programming tools can use many gigabytes each.

When everything you are using fits comfortably in RAM, the processor can work at full speed. When it does not fit, the operating system starts using a trick called **virtual memory**: it moves the parts of memory you have not touched recently out to storage (to a "page file" on Windows, "swap" on macOS and Linux) and brings them back when needed. On an SSD this works tolerably; on an old hard drive it is painfully slow. Either way, it is far slower than real RAM. Phones handle the same problem differently: they quietly close apps in the background, which is why an app you left a few minutes ago sometimes restarts from scratch when you return to it.

But here is the important nuance: **RAM you do not use does nothing for you.** If your work needs 10 GB and you have 16 GB, upgrading to 64 GB will not make anything noticeably faster. Extra RAM is like a bigger desk: it helps only if you were running out of desk.

You may also notice that your operating system shows RAM as "almost full" even when you are doing little. That is usually not a problem. Modern systems deliberately use spare RAM to cache files and apps you are likely to open, because empty RAM is wasted RAM. The cached data is thrown away instantly when a program actually needs the space.

## ROM: the memory that was meant never to change

### Read-only, literally

**ROM** stands for **read-only memory**. In its original form, it was exactly that: the data was physically built into the chip when it was manufactured, in a process called *mask ROM*. The chip could be read forever, it kept its contents without any power, and nobody could change them. Old game cartridges for consoles worked this way: the game was literally part of the chip's wiring.

Why would anyone want memory that cannot be changed? Because every computing device faces a chicken-and-egg problem when it is switched on. RAM is empty (it forgot everything when the power went off). Storage is full of useful software, but the processor needs instructions to know how to talk to the storage in the first place. Something has to provide those very first instructions, and it must be there the instant power arrives. That something is a small non-volatile memory holding the **firmware**: the low-level code that wakes up the hardware, checks it, and starts loading the operating system.

### From ROM to flash: memory that is "mostly read"

Pure mask ROM had an obvious drawback: if the code had a bug, the only fix was to replace the chip. So engineers developed a family of memories that keep their contents without power but *can* be rewritten, with increasing convenience:

1. **PROM** (programmable ROM): blank when made, and written once by "blowing" tiny fuses. After that, it is permanent.
2. **EPROM** (erasable PROM): could be erased by shining strong ultraviolet light through a small quartz window on top of the chip, then reprogrammed. Old circuit boards often have chips with a little round window covered by a sticker to stop stray sunlight from erasing them.
3. **EEPROM** (electrically erasable PROM): can be erased and rewritten electrically, byte by byte, without removing the chip, but slowly and only a limited number of times.
4. **Flash memory**: a descendant of EEPROM that erases data in large blocks at once, which makes it far faster and cheaper per bit.

Flash memory was invented by Fujio Masuoka and colleagues at Toshiba. They presented NOR flash in 1984 and NAND flash in 1987. The name reportedly came from a colleague who said the erasing process reminded him of a camera flash.

Today, the firmware in your laptop (the BIOS or its modern successor, **UEFI**) usually lives on a small flash chip on the motherboard. It is technically rewritable, and you can "update the BIOS", but in normal use it is only read. So engineers sometimes still call it ROM in the loose sense: memory that is non-volatile and *mostly* read-only.

### NOR and NAND: two flavours of flash

The two types Masuoka invented divide the work between them:

- **NOR flash** allows fast random reads of individual bytes, so a processor can run code directly from it. It is ideal for firmware, but it is relatively expensive per gigabyte. Firmware chips are typically only a few to a few dozen megabytes.
- **NAND flash** reads and writes in pages and erases in larger blocks. It cannot easily run code in place, but it packs data far more densely and cheaply. NAND is what fills SSDs, USB sticks, memory cards and the storage in every smartphone.

And that brings us to the phone spec sheet.

## Why your phone says "ROM" when it means storage

When a phone listing says "8 GB RAM / 256 GB ROM", the "ROM" is the phone's internal storage: NAND flash, where Android or iOS, your apps, photos and messages live. It is entirely rewritable; you write to it every time you take a picture. Calling it "read-only" memory is, strictly speaking, wrong.

The habit has understandable roots. Early phones and devices often stored their operating system in genuinely read-only or rarely-written memory, separate from the small amount of user space. The Android modding community has long used "ROM" to mean an operating system image (as in "flashing a custom ROM"), because that image used to sit in the read-only system partition. Over time, sellers, especially in Asian markets, started using "ROM" for the whole internal storage. Apple, Samsung and Google generally write "storage" in their own specifications, but the "RAM/ROM" style remains common in shop listings and on many brands' boxes.

None of this matters much as long as you translate it correctly:

- **"RAM" on a phone** = working memory. Determines how many apps can stay open in the background without reloading and how smoothly heavy apps run.
- **"ROM" on a phone** = storage. Determines how many apps, photos, videos and files you can keep.

A phone with 12 GB RAM and 128 GB "ROM" is good at multitasking but may fill up quickly if you shoot a lot of video. One with 6 GB RAM and 512 GB "ROM" can hold an enormous library but may reload apps more often.

### A note on "virtual RAM" and "RAM extension"

Many Android phones now advertise something like "8 GB + 8 GB extended RAM". The second number is not extra RAM chips. It is a portion of the storage set aside to act as swap space, the same virtual-memory trick computers use. It can help keep a few more background apps alive, but storage is far slower than real RAM, so it is not equivalent. When comparing phones, look at the physical RAM figure.

## Storage: the big, slow, permanent filing cabinet

### Hard disk drives

For decades, computer storage meant the **hard disk drive** (HDD): spinning magnetic platters, with a read/write head on an arm floating a hair's breadth above the surface. HDDs are cheap per terabyte and still used for bulk storage, backups and servers holding huge archives. But because they involve moving parts, finding a piece of data takes several milliseconds while the platter rotates and the arm moves. Sustained transfer speeds for typical consumer hard drives are in the range of roughly 100 to 250 megabytes per second.

### Solid-state drives

A **solid-state drive** (SSD) stores data on NAND flash chips with no moving parts. That alone makes it dramatically faster at finding data, quieter, more shock-resistant and more power-efficient.

SSDs come in a few forms:

- **SATA SSDs** use the same connection as older hard drives and top out at around 550 MB/s because of the limits of that interface.
- **NVMe SSDs** connect over PCI Express, the high-speed lanes the graphics card also uses. A PCIe 4.0 NVMe drive can read at around 7,000 MB/s; PCIe 5.0 drives roughly double that on paper.
- Phones use embedded flash standards such as **UFS**, which follow the same idea in a compact, low-power package.

### Putting the speeds side by side

The numbers are easier to feel if we compare how long it takes to fetch one small piece of data (latency), using rough orders of magnitude:

- **CPU cache (SRAM)**: around a nanosecond or a few nanoseconds.
- **Main memory (DRAM)**: on the order of 100 nanoseconds.
- **NVMe SSD**: tens of microseconds, which is hundreds of times slower than DRAM.
- **Hard disk**: several milliseconds, which is roughly a hundred times slower again.

If fetching from cache took one second, fetching from RAM would take a couple of minutes, from an SSD a few days, and from a hard disk several months. That is why the operating system works so hard to keep what you need in RAM, and why swapping to a slow disk feels like the computer has frozen.

### Flash wears out (slowly)

Each NAND flash cell can only be erased and rewritten a limited number of times before it becomes unreliable. Manufacturers squeeze more bits into each cell to cut cost: SLC stores one bit per cell, MLC two, TLC three, QLC four. More bits per cell means cheaper, denser storage but generally lower endurance and slower sustained writing.

For ordinary users this is rarely a practical concern. SSD controllers spread writes evenly across cells (*wear levelling*), keep spare cells in reserve, and drives are rated for many hundreds of terabytes written. A typical person writing a few dozen gigabytes a day would take many years to approach that. Heavy video editors or people running databases should look at the endurance rating, usually given as **TBW** (terabytes written).

One practical tip: SSDs, especially cheap ones, often slow down when they are nearly full, because the controller has less free space to shuffle data around. Leaving 10 to 20 percent free is a sensible habit.

## What happens when you press the power button

Following one ordinary start-up shows how the three kinds of memory cooperate.

1. **Power arrives.** RAM is empty: whatever was in it yesterday drained away seconds after shutdown. The processor wakes up knowing only one thing: a fixed address where it should look for its first instruction. That address points into the firmware chip.
2. **Firmware runs.** The UEFI firmware, read from its small flash chip, checks that the processor, memory and essential hardware are present and working. On many PCs this includes "training" the RAM: testing timings so the memory can run reliably at its rated speed. This is why a new computer, or one with freshly installed RAM, sometimes takes noticeably longer to start the first time.
3. **Firmware finds the storage.** It locates the SSD, reads a small boot program from it and loads that program into RAM.
4. **The operating system loads.** The boot program loads the core of Windows, macOS, Linux or Android from storage into RAM, piece by piece. From now on the processor runs mostly from RAM, fetching from storage only when it needs something new.
5. **You open an app.** The app's code and data are copied from storage into RAM. The first launch after a restart is slower than later ones because later launches can reuse what is already cached in RAM.
6. **You shut down.** Anything you saved is already in storage. Anything only in RAM, such as an unsaved document, disappears. The firmware stays on its chip, unchanged, ready for tomorrow.

Phones follow the same pattern with different names: a boot ROM inside the processor chip, a bootloader stored in flash, then the operating system loaded from the phone's storage into RAM.

## Two specialised kinds of RAM worth knowing

**ECC memory.** Very rarely, a bit in RAM flips by accident, for example because of electrical noise or even a stray particle from cosmic radiation. For a home user, a single flipped bit might crash a program or, more often, go unnoticed. For a server running a bank's database for years without a restart, it matters. **Error-correcting code** (ECC) memory stores a few extra bits with each chunk of data so that single-bit errors can be detected and fixed automatically. It is standard in servers and workstations and uncommon in consumer laptops. (DDR5 chips include some error correction inside the chip itself, but that is not the same as full ECC across the whole memory system.)

**Unified memory.** Apple's M-series Macs and many phone chips put the processor and graphics on one chip and let them share a single pool of RAM, rather than giving the graphics card its own separate memory. This avoids copying data back and forth and can be very efficient. It also means the one RAM figure must serve both the CPU and the graphics, which is one reason heavy creative users of these machines often choose larger memory configurations. And because that memory is part of the chip package, it cannot be upgraded later.

## Clearing up common myths

**"More RAM means more space for my files."** No. RAM is cleared every time you shut down. Files live in storage. If your phone says "storage full", buying a phone with more RAM will not help; you need more storage.

**"ROM on my phone can't be changed."** The "ROM" figure on phone boxes is ordinary rewritable storage. You change it every time you install an app.

**"Closing apps on my phone frees RAM and saves battery."** Usually not. Modern Android and iOS manage memory themselves. Swiping away apps forces them to start from scratch next time, which can use *more* energy. Close an app if it is misbehaving, not as a habit.

**"My RAM is 90 percent used, something is wrong."** Often nothing is wrong. Operating systems fill spare RAM with cached data on purpose, and release it the moment a program needs it. Worry only if the computer is actually slow and the disk is constantly busy.

**"Bill Gates said 640 KB ought to be enough for anybody."** This famous quote, supposedly about the memory limit of the original IBM PC in 1981, has never been traced to a reliable source, and Gates has denied saying it. It survives because it captures a real truth: every generation underestimates how much memory the next generation of software will want.

## How much do you actually need?

The right numbers depend on what you do and change over time as software grows. As of the mid-2020s, these are reasonable starting points. Treat them as guides, not rules.

### Laptops and desktops

For **RAM**:

- **8 GB**: the bare minimum for Windows or macOS with light use (web, documents, video calls). Microsoft's official minimum for Windows 11 is just 4 GB, but in practice that is painfully tight. With many browser tabs open, 8 GB fills up quickly.
- **16 GB**: the comfortable choice for most people, including students, office work with many apps open, light photo editing and casual gaming.
- **32 GB**: for heavy work: large photo or video editing, music production with many tracks, software development with virtual machines or containers, serious gaming, big spreadsheets and data analysis.
- **64 GB or more**: professional video editing at high resolution, 3D rendering, large scientific or AI models run locally, many virtual machines at once.

For **storage**:

- **256 GB** fills up surprisingly fast once the operating system, updates, a few large apps and a photo library are installed.
- **512 GB** is a sensible minimum for most people buying today.
- **1 TB or more** if you keep large media libraries, games (many modern games are 50 to 150 GB each) or video projects. An external drive or cloud storage can supplement a smaller internal drive for archives.

Always prefer an **SSD** (ideally NVMe) for the drive the operating system lives on. Of all the upgrades you can make to an older computer, swapping a hard drive for an SSD usually produces the most dramatic difference in how fast it feels.

### Phones

For **RAM**, current mid-range and flagship phones typically ship with 8 to 16 GB. 8 GB is comfortable for most people; more helps heavy multitaskers and mobile gamers, and is increasingly used by on-device AI features. Below 6 GB, expect apps to reload more often.

For **storage** ("ROM"), think about how you take photos and video. If you shoot 4K video regularly, 128 GB fills up fast. 256 GB is a comfortable middle ground for most people; 512 GB or more if your phone is your main camera and you do not like managing cloud backups. Check whether the phone has a microSD slot, since many recent phones do not.

### Check before you buy: can it be upgraded?

This is one of the most practical points in this whole guide. On many modern laptops, especially thin models, the RAM is **soldered** to the motherboard (common with LPDDR memory). You will never be able to add more. If a laptop has soldered RAM, buy the amount you will need for the entire life of the machine, not just today. Some laptops have one soldered bank and one free slot; some have two free slots. The storage drive is more often replaceable, usually as an M.2 NVMe stick, but not always. Phones cannot be upgraded at all.

Memory prices also move a lot. Since late 2025, strong demand for memory from AI data centres has pushed DRAM and flash prices sharply higher, and many manufacturers have raised the price of RAM upgrades or held back on capacity. That makes choosing the right configuration at purchase even more important.

## Three quick scenarios

**A student who mostly writes essays, browses and watches lectures.** A laptop with 16 GB RAM and a 512 GB SSD will feel smooth for years. 8 GB will work but may struggle with many tabs and a video call at once.

**A freelance designer editing photos and short videos.** 32 GB RAM, ideally upgradable, and at least 1 TB of NVMe SSD, plus an external drive for archives. If the RAM is soldered, do not settle for 16 GB.

**A phone buyer choosing between 8 GB RAM / 256 GB and 12 GB RAM / 128 GB at the same price.** For most people, the 256 GB version is the safer bet: running out of storage is a daily annoyance, while 8 GB of RAM is already enough for typical use. The 12 GB version makes sense mainly for heavy gamers who keep their media in the cloud.

## A short glossary

- **Bit / byte**: a bit is a single 0 or 1; a byte is 8 bits.
- **Cache**: a small, very fast memory (usually SRAM) inside or near the processor.
- **DRAM**: dynamic RAM, the main memory in computers and phones; needs constant refreshing.
- **Firmware**: low-level software stored in non-volatile memory that starts the hardware.
- **Flash**: rewritable non-volatile memory that erases in blocks; NOR for code, NAND for storage.
- **NVMe**: a fast protocol for SSDs over PCI Express.
- **Non-volatile**: keeps its data without power (ROM, flash, hard drives).
- **Swap / page file**: storage space used as overflow when RAM is full.
- **UEFI / BIOS**: the firmware that starts a PC.
- **Volatile**: loses its data when power is removed (RAM).

## The takeaway

The words are confusing because history piled them up: RAM named for a property most memory now shares, ROM named for chips that today can mostly be rewritten, and a phone industry that borrowed "ROM" to mean storage. But the underlying picture is simple. The processor works on a fast, forgetful desk (RAM). It keeps everything else in a large, slower filing cabinet (storage). And a small, rarely-changed rulebook (firmware in ROM or flash) tells it how to start the day.

When you next read "8 GB RAM / 256 GB ROM", you will know the first number is how much you can work on at once and the second is how much you can keep. And when you buy a laptop, you will know to ask the one question that matters most for its long-term usefulness: can the memory be upgraded later?
